sources.entry: OpenZiti - Fully-featured, zero trust, full mesh overlay network. Includes a 2FA support out of the box, clients for all major desktop/mobile OS'es. (Source Code) Apache-2.0 Go

summary.one_liner: OpenZiti is an open-source zero-trust overlay networking platform that makes network services dark (no listening ports) and reachable only by cryptographically authenticated, policy-authorized identities.
summary.what_it_does: The README describes a controller (identity issuance with x509 certificates, policy enforcement, REST API and web admin console) and a mesh of edge routers that carry end-to-end encrypted traffic between endpoints. Endpoints are either SDKs (Go, C, Python, Node.js, Java, Swift, C#) embedded in applications, or tunnelers (Linux, Windows, macOS, iOS, Android) that route unmodified software through the overlay. Services make outbound connections to routers and register themselves, so they expose no inbound ports. Access is checked per service, and revoking a policy terminates active connections. Quick starts cover a Docker compose stack and the ziti CLI with `ziti edge quickstart`, plus installing the Ziti Admin Console.
use_cases: replace VPN access to internal services
hide APIs and services from the internet
connect Kubernetes clusters or VMs without VPN tunnels
access self-hosted home lab services like Nextcloud or Home Assistant remotely
give IoT devices and machines unique cryptographic identities
secure agent and MCP server communication
how_to_run: Download the ziti binary from GitHub Releases
stack: C, Python, Node.js, Java, Swift, C# SDKs
notable: Dark services with zero listening ports; services make outbound connections only
Three deployment models: network access, host access via tunnelers, and in-process SDK access
Per-service policy authorization with real-time revocation of active connections
Tunnelers for Linux, Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android that need no code changes
Managed offering available from NetFoundry, the project's sponsor
caveats: README points to separate product documentation for production deployments; quick starts are aimed at development, testing, and learning
Application-level (SDK) access requires code changes; tunnelers cover existing software but encrypt only tunneler-to-tunneler or tunneler-to-SDK paths
Some README links are missing their URLs, so setup details must be taken from the external docs
